### Reviewer 3

Through combined theoretical and experimental investigations Li et al. study the quantum dynamics of the three-atom reactive scattering H + D2 --> HD + D at a collision energy of 2.38 eV that lies below the conical interaction of the ground and excited state of the three atom (H3) potential. They analyze the high resolution scattering angular distribution of state specific (v’, j’) product HD using rigorous quantum dynamical and quasi classical trajectory calculations. The experimentally observed oscillations in the angular distribution that arises from the interference between the direct and the looping pathways around the conical intersection of the three atom potential tallies with theory only when the topological phase effect is included in the calculation. A clear phase shift of the oscillatory structure of the measured angular distribution relative to that calculated excluding the GP effect clearly illustrates how the geometrical phase controls this reactive scattering.

To gain deeper understanding they focus on the specific product state HD (v’=3, j’=12) that has strong contribution to the observed sideways scattering. Detailed partial wave analysis reveal that oscillations observed in the forward and sideways scattering distribution are mainly due to the interference effect between the direct path (path 1) of the higher partial waves and the looping path (path 2) of the lower partial waves (J<15). The back scattering from path 2 contributed mainly by the higher order partial waves is in stark contrast to the conventional scattering theory, and thus, provides a strong signature of the quantum phase effect of this reaction pathway that goes circling around the conical intersection. The partial wave analysis analysis further reveals the detailed dynamics of H atom insertion via the two transition states of path 2. It exhibits roaming like behavior of the H-atom around the D-atoms which is facilitated by the bond stretching of the D2 molecule. This raises further interesting question, whether prior vibrational excitation of the reactant will favor the looping path, thus enhancing the topological phase effect.

The combined experimental and theoretical studies of this particular H + D2 reaction have been carried out before [Refs 27-31], however, these investigations failed to detect the geometrical phase effect. The present work clearly demonstrates the topological phase effect in this specific three atom reaction, which is new. However, the GP effects from the interference of the direct and the looping reaction paths in an isotopic variant reaction H + HD --> H2 +D has been demonstrated multiple times by the same group of authors [Refs 16, 20, 21], and these quantum dynamical studies are closely parallel to the current work. In this sense the current study is more of an extension of their previous works. The strength of the present work lies in their rigorous theoretical analysis of the experimental scattering angular distribution via discrimination of the partial wave contributions. The partial wave analysis manifests the quantum nature of the looping path. It reveals the roaming like behavior of path 2 and shows how the insertion dynamics proceeds via transient vibrational excitation of the D2 molecule.

Although these results could be published in a suitable journal, in my mind, it lacks sufficient novelty to justify publication in Nature Communication.

### Reviewer 4

This manuscript presents a joint experimental and theoretical study on the hydrogen exchange reaction, H + D2 → HD + D, focusing on geometric phase-induced quantum interference effects. These are attributed to interference between the direct abstraction and roaming insertion pathways.

The roaming insertion pathway shows an interesting effect: low-partial-wave collisions preferentially lead to forward scattering, whereas high-partial-wave collisions mostly lead to backward scattering. The opposite is generally observed, and is also the case for the direct abstraction pathway in this manuscript.

The roaming insertion pathway has been investigated in more detail using quasi-classical trajectory calculations, offering valuable insight in the underlying reaction mechanisms.

In previous beautiful studies on H + HD, an isotopic variant of the same reaction, geometric phase effects have been reported and analysed (refs 16, 20, 21, 26 and Yuan et al., Nat. Comm. 11, 3640 (2020), which to our surprise has not been cited in this work). In these cases, they showed up as angular oscillations in either the forward or backward scattered directions. As mentioned by the authors on page 4, numerous experimental studies have investigated the H + D2 system already, but until now, geometric phase effects have not been observed.

The experimental image recorded for this work, in a similar way as in previous work by the same research groups, is beautiful and of extremely high quality. Oscillations are clearly visible in the angular scattering distributions for angles between 0-70 degrees (sideways scattering). Fig. 2 very convincingly shows that these oscillations are due to geometric phase effects. This manuscript therefore presents the first observation of the geometric phase effect for H + D2.

Using QCT calculations, the origin of these oscillations has been investigated, and it was found that a roaming insertion pathway is involved, as was also seen for H + HD (ref. 21 for instance). This pathway has been investigated in a more detailed way, and the underlying mechanism has been clarified.

This manuscript presents beautiful and high-quality work that in our opinion clearly has the potential to be published in Nature Communications. However, to strengthen the clarity of the manuscript and to more clearly highlight the novelty of the current findings – especially with respect to previous work on H + HD by the same groups – we ask the authors to address the following points. We believe this is crucial before the manuscript can be considered for acceptance in Nature Communications.

- We recommend that the authors revise the last part of the manuscript, which discusses the underlying dynamics of the observed phenomenon (starting from page 11) to make it more accessible to a broader audience, including non-specialists.
- While Fig. 2 presents oscillations for two different rings, the manuscript afterwards focusses exclusively on the mechanisms underlying the oscillatory structures shown in panel a, without addressing the oscillations shown in panel b. We think the authors should extend their analysis to include the oscillations shown in panel b. Does the newly identified roaming insertion mechanism also play a role in this case? If so, this would further strengthen the findings. This is particularly important as the final vibrational states of the HD product is different in panel b compared to panel a.
- We ask the authors to more clearly show and highlight the difference between the roaming insertion mechanisms found for H + HD and H + D2. On page 13, the authors write that the roaming mechanism for H + D2 relies on a symmetric stretch mode, which is absent in the H + HD system. This is a particularly compelling conclusion that would clearly distinguish the present study from previous work. We suggest that the authors clearly show that this is the case, for instance by demonstrating that the roaming mechanism responsible for oscillations in the backward direction for H + HD does not play a role for H + D2. Analogously, the authors can show that the newly identified roaming mechanism is really absent in H + HD (also at sidescattered angles where the theoretical DCS in H+HD shows clear oscillations as well. Are these sidescattered oscillations in H+HD indeed fundamentally different than the sidescattered oscillations found in this work for H + D2?).
Ideally, one would like to see plots like Figure 3,4,5,S6 and S7 for the H + D2 and H + HD systems next to each other to clearly illustrate the differences in interpretation of the roaming mechanisms involved.

Smaller comments, questions and suggestions:
- On page 5, the authors refer to Supplementary Note 1 for experimental details regarding the ionization of the D-atom products. However, there is no information on the ionization scheme in this note, nor in the Methods section. This, and additional information about how the image in Fig. 1 is measured, should be included.
